content: The capitalization of titles and headings is governed by various style guides, including the Gregg Reference Manual, the Chicago Manual of Style (Chicago Style), the American Psychological Association (APA Style), and the Modern Language Association (MLA Style). Each guide provides specific rules for capitalization, which are outlined below. General Recommendations for Capitalization 1. Always capitalize the first word of every new sentence or bullet point. Example: Heart failure is defined as the inability of the heart to pump enough blood to meet the demands of the body. Example (Bullet): Headache. 2. Capitalize the names of diseases named after individuals but not general disease names. Example: The patient is suffering from Münchausen syndrome but has no symptoms of major depressive disorder. 3. Capitalize trade names of medications but not their generic names. Example: The preferred drug for the symptoms of this disease is Tylenol, which contains acetaminophen. 4. Capitalize abbreviations. Example: Chickenpox is caused by varicella zoster virus (VZV). Example: The United States Preventive Task Force (USPSTF) has established guidelines for screening various diseases. 5. Capitalize names of individuals, cities, countries, races, or study designs. Example: In 1836, Joseph Parrish described three cases of severe lower urinary tract symptoms without the presence of a bladder stone. Example: Pyelonephritis is more prevalent among the Asian population compared to Caucasians. Example: New information suggests that elements of heart failure in African Americans and Caucasians may be different. Example: A study conducted in Olmsted County, Minnesota, showed that the incidence of heart failure (ICD9/428) has not declined during two decades, but survival after onset has increased overall, with less improvement among women and elderly persons. Example: Data from the NHLBI’s Framingham Heart Study indicate that heart failure (HF) incidence approaches 10 per 1,000 population after age 65. 6. Capitalize headings. Example: Country Specific Causes. Example: Natural History, Complications, and Prognosis. Gregg Reference Manual 1. Capitalize all words in titles except: Articles such as a, an, and the. Short conjunctions such as and, as, but, if, or, and nor. Short prepositions such as at, by, for, in, of, off, on, out, to, and up. 2. Exceptions: Always capitalize the first and last words of titles, regardless of their length. Capitalize the word the at the beginning of a title only if it is part of the title. Capitalize the first word following a dash or colon in a title. Capitalize words such as in, out, off, up, and by in titles when they serve as adverbs rather than prepositions. Capitalize short prepositions such as up, in, on, and for when used together with prepositions having four or more letters. Chicago Manual of Style 1. Capitalize the first and last words in titles and subtitles, as well as all other major words (nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, and some conjunctions). 2. Lowercase articles (the, a, an). 3. Lowercase prepositions, regardless of length, except when used adverbially or adjectivally (e.g., Look Up, Turn Down, The On Button). 4. Lowercase conjunctions (and, but, for, or, nor). 5. Lowercase to in infinitives (e.g., to Run, to Hide). 6. Lowercase parts of proper names that would be lowercased in text, such as de or von. 7. Lowercase the second part of a species name, such as fulvescens in Acipenser fulvescens, even if it is the last word in a title or subtitle. APA Style 1. Capitalize the first word in a complete sentence. 2. Capitalize the first word after a colon that begins a complete sentence. 3. Capitalize major words in titles of books and articles within the body of the paper. 4. Conjunctions, articles, and short prepositions are not considered major words; however, capitalize all words of four letters or more. 5. Capitalize all verbs (including linking verbs), nouns, adjectives, adverbs, and pronouns. 6. When a capitalized word is a hyphenated compound, capitalize both words. 7. Capitalize the first word after a colon or a dash in a title. 8. Capitalize proper nouns and adjectives and words used as proper nouns. Proper adjectives that have acquired a common meaning are not capitalized (consult Merriam-Webster's Collegiate Dictionary for guidance). 9. Capitalize names of university departments if they refer to a specific department within a specific university and complete names of academic courses if they refer to a specific course. 10. Capitalize trade and brand names of drugs, equipment, and food. 11. Capitalize nouns followed by numerals or letters that denote a specific place in a numbered series. 12. Capitalize exact, complete titles of published and unpublished tests. Words such as test or scale are not capitalized if they refer to subscales of tests. 13. Capitalize names of derived variables within a factor or principal components analysis. The words factor and component are not capitalized unless followed by a number. MLA Style 1. In a title or subtitle, capitalize the first word, the last word, and all principal words, including those that follow hyphens in compound terms. 2. Capitalize the following parts of speech: Nouns Pronouns Verbs Adjectives Adverbs Articles Prepositions Coordinating conjunctions The to in infinitives Hyphenated Words 1. Gregg Reference Manual: In a heading or title, capitalize all elements except articles (a, an, the), short prepositions (at, by, for, in, of, off, on, out, to, up), and short conjunctions (and, as, but, if, or, nor). 2. Chicago Manual of Style: Always capitalize the first element. Capitalize any subsequent elements unless they are articles, prepositions, coordinating conjunctions (and, but, for, or, nor), or modifiers such as flat or sharp following musical key symbols. If the first element is merely a prefix or combining form that could not stand alone as a word (e.g., anti, pre), do not capitalize the second element unless it is a proper noun or proper adjective. Do not capitalize the second element in a hyphenated spelled-out number (e.g., Run-ins and Take-offs).
